text: Season two opens in Busan, at four in the morning, on a breakwater a kilometre long.
Jaeha staggers along it in Auntie Geum's spare tracksuit, while she rides beside him on a moped, yelling through a newspaper. Lift those knees, noodle.
Behind him, Lyra jogs backwards without breaking a sweat. Why run if nothing is chasing them? Nib: something is always chasing.
At the lighthouse, Jaeha collapses face-first onto the concrete.
Borro scoops him up like a sack of rice. He'll carry him home.
Geum points the newspaper at him like a sword. Put him down. Summons don't carry the Operator.
The Operator carries for them, so the Operator gets strong. Flat on his back, Jaeha admits it's a very good rule.
A window: day one of the quest. Carry capacity, one hundred percent. Body rating, F.
Dawn comes up over the harbour, and he walks back on his own feet.
Five a.m.: the fish market, and the next order on Geum's list. Carry ice.
Three market aunties start a betting pool. Ten thousand won says he drops the third crate. Another says he won't reach two.
His arms shake under the first crate.
It hits the floor in an explosion of ice and mackerel, and the aunties pay each other.
Borro strolls past with four crates on one shoulder. The aunties decide the big one can stay forever.
Lyra holds her nose at an octopus that won't stop staring. Behind her, Nib quietly steals a fish cake.
Geum slaps another crate into Jaeha's arms. His arms are shaking? Good. That means they're working.
A small window: capacity, up four tenths of a percent.
Jaeha's eyes narrow. He reads windows like contracts.
And here's the small print. Capacity grows with sustained load. Peak load does nothing.
It doesn't care how heavy. It cares how long.
So he asks Geum for something different: not the heaviest thing, but the thing he can hold the longest.
Geum's gold tooth slowly appears.
An hour later, he's still sitting on a tub with a tray of ice level on his arms, writing in his notebook. The aunties wonder if it's a novel.
And the number jumps: one hundred to one hundred and four percent.
Geum turns away so nobody sees her face. Head S-rank, she mutters.
Six a.m.: tteokbokki in the orange tent, with Borro's head poking in through the flap.
Geum sets a stool and a bowl of soup in front of Nib. Sit, soldier. You've stood enough.
She can tell he held a wall once, just by the way he stands. Nib's ears twitch.
On a video call, Seoa ties her school tie and reminds him the budget says home by Friday. Dinner at seven, he promises.
Then Bomi calls, begging to come down and stream the Trap Rats in Busan. Geum takes the phone. No cameras in her tent.
She hangs up. Click.
Seven a.m., one more set. Lyra wades into the surf to wash off the fish market, wringing out her silver braid in the sunrise.
Two fishermen drop their net in the sea, and Jaeha, hauling a sack of rice, walks straight into a lamppost. Nib says nothing.
Across the harbour road, a black car sits in the shade with its engine off.
Han Sora, binoculars up, reports to Director Baek. His hands still shake, and an old woman has him carrying fish. Baek: let him carry, and keep watching.
On her other wrist, a brand-new compass leans toward the harbour.
That afternoon, dead fish line the shore under the breakwater.
Their scales shimmer violet along a thin dark crack.
Third day running, a fisherman tells Geum. The sea keeps spitting them out. She doesn't answer.
Her steel fingers twitch on their own.
And Jaeha's warning window comes back. A sealed gate is failing, somewhere near.
So he asks her straight. The man she saw ten years ago. Who was he?
Geum does not turn. One more set.
That's not an answer, he says. It's the only one he's getting today.
Tuesday, four a.m. He's still slow, but this time he runs the whole breakwater upright.
He carries a full cup of tteokbokki, and the sauce barely moves.
Capacity, one hundred and seven percent. Body rating, still F.
Lyra's verdict: still garbage. Geum's: slightly less garbage.
In the afternoon, Geum makes Nib and Lyra spar in field form while Jaeha carries every blow, two summons, his limit, for nine minutes and forty seconds, nose bleeding.
That night, he sits with Nib under the lighthouse. Nib says the sea sounds wrong. A wall sounds like that before it falls.
And Nib is spent. Outside a gate, his field form won't come back for three hours.
Geum shuts the tent and yells down the breakwater: bed. Four o'clock comes early.
Near midnight, only one old fisherman is left out on the tetrapods.
The water at his feet starts to bubble, and glow violet.
Something drags itself out of the sea: a crab's claws, an eel's tail, a mouth full of needles.
The fisherman screams.
Jaeha runs for him, calling Nib. But Nib has no field form for three hours.
So Jaeha shoves the fisherman clear and takes the claw across his own arm.
On his back, he watches it rear over him, and a second claw rise out of the water behind it.
Then a pair of pink rubber slippers steps in front of him. Get behind me, kid.
Auntie Geum, sixty-two, faces the monster with a ladle, and the sea behind it starts to glow.
